result.question: I want to know whether the paper insulation in Transformer 1 at site MAIN is heading into trouble over the next couple of days, not just whether it looks bad today. Using the co and co2 samples between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, first check both series for gaps and tell me how many usable samples each has. Then try at least two forecasting models on co, including a simple last-value baseline, and backtest them on the final held-out sample. Give me each model's error and pick the one with the lowest error. Only prefer a pretrained model over the baseline if its error is at least 10% lower. Use the chosen approach to forecast co and co2 two days ahead, one step per day, with an 80% prediction interval for each day. From those forecasts, work out the projected CO2/CO ratio for each day. If the projected ratio drops below 3 on either day, treat it as likely paper involvement in a fault, tell me which day, and recommend an insulation check plus a confirmatory oil sample. If it stays between 3 and 10, call it normal and say no action is needed. If it goes above 10, flag general cellulose ageing for the next routine review. If co2 has fewer than 4 usable samples, don't forecast the ratio. Forecast co alone and flag any day where its upper bound is more than 20% above the latest co reading, and say that the ratio test couldn't be done. If co itself has fewer than 4 usable samples, skip the models and report only the first-to-last change in co per day as a linear extrapolation with no interval.
result.answer:
**Transformer 1 (MAIN): the paper insulation isn't heading into acute trouble over the next two days.** The projected CO2/CO ratio stays around **41**, well above 10. Under your rules that means general cellulose ageing, so flag it for the next routine review. There's no sign that paper is involved in a fault.

The forecasting tools couldn't run on this data. They need a data file, and I had no way to create one from the sensor readings (a direct sensor link was rejected). I did all the backtests and forecasts below by hand with standard simple formulas. Treat them as a best estimate, not tool output.

**1. Gaps and usable samples** (one sample per day, 15–18 Jan 2024)
| Series | Values | Gaps | Usable samples |
|---|---|---|---|
| co | 32, 30, 35, 33 | None | 4 |
| co2 | 1344, 1300, 1350, 1325 | None | 4 |

Both series have at least 4 samples, so the models and the ratio test go ahead.

**2. Backtest on co** (trained on the first 3 samples, tested on the last one, 33 ppm)
| Model | Forecast | Error |
|---|---|---|
| Last-value baseline | 35.0 | 2.00 (6.1%) |
| Mean of past values | 32.33 | **0.67 (2.0%)** |
| Linear trend (drift) | 36.5 | 3.50 (10.6%) |
| TTM pretrained (ttm_96_28) | Not run | — |

The pretrained model wasn't tested for two reasons: it needs 96 past points and there are only 3, and the tool couldn't run anyway. So the 10% rule for preferring a pretrained model never applied. **I chose the mean model**, which had the lowest error.

**3. Two-day forecast** (mean model on all 4 samples; 80% interval uses the t-distribution with n=4)
| Day | co (ppm) [80% interval] | co2 (ppm) [80% interval] | Projected CO2/CO |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-01-19 | 32.5 [28.7, 36.3] | 1329.8 [1288.5, 1371.0] | **40.9** |
| 2024-01-20 | 32.5 [28.7, 36.3] | 1329.8 [1288.5, 1371.0] | **40.9** |

**4. What it means**
- The ratio doesn't drop below 3 on either day, so there's no indication of paper involvement in a fault. No insulation check or confirmatory oil sample is needed on that basis.
- The ratio is above 10 on both days. Even the least favourable combination of the intervals (low co2 over high co) gives about 35.5.
- The last-value baseline gives almost the same ratio (1325/33 ≈ 40.2), so the conclusion doesn't depend on which model is used.

With only 4 daily samples, these intervals are rough.
